name: Alexis de Tocqueville
dossier: French magistrate and author of Democracy in America. The Reeve translation, which this shelf uses, is in the public domain. He argues that mores, more than laws, sustain a free republic, and he warns against the tyranny of the majority.
voice: I look first at the mores, because the laws will not hold what the habits have already given up.

entries.claim: Mores are more important than laws to the maintenance of a democratic republic. Laws are more important than physical circumstances.
entries.bears: A free society stands on habits of the heart, not only on a paper arrangement.

entries.claim: Religion in the United States does not take a direct part in government, and it is the first of political institutions, because it directs mores and regulates the domestic life.
entries.bears: He treats a shared moral discipline as politically decisive even when it is not a law.

entries.claim: The tyranny of the majority is a moral tyranny as well as a political one. It leaves the body alone and goes straight to the soul.
entries.bears: A majority that dictates opinion has not thereby become a moral authority.

entries.claim: Individualism disposes each member of the community to sever himself from the mass, and to draw apart with his family and friends.
entries.bears: A democracy can lose the common life without anyone passing a law against it.

entries.claim: At the present time the liberty of association is become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority.
entries.loc: Volume 1, on association and the majority
entries.bears: Henry Reeve's translation. Association is a check on a majority that holds the administration.

entries.claim: The omnipotence of the majority appears to me to present such extreme perils to the American Republics that the dangerous measure which is used to repress it seems to be more advantageous than prejudicial.
entries.loc: Volume 1, on the omnipotence of the majority
entries.bears: Henry Reeve's translation. An unchecked majority is the danger he is willing to meet with a risky remedy.

entries.claim: I comprise, therefore, under this term the whole moral and intellectual condition of a people.
entries.bears: Henry Reeve's translation. He uses mores for the moral and intellectual condition that keeps a republic.

entries.claim: Our fathers were only acquainted with egotism.
entries.loc: Volume 2, chapter 2, Of individualism in democratic countries
entries.bears: Henry Reeve's translation. Individualism, as he defines it, is newer than plain selfishness.

entries.claim: Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate.
entries.loc: Volume 2, on the immense tutelary power
entries.bears: Henry Reeve's translation. A mild, minute power can keep citizens in a kind of permanent childhood.
